---
title: "Text Recovery Workflow"
---

## Tesseract-based process

The workflow for this project assumes OCR is used as a first-pass recovery tool rather than a final authoritative copy. The process is:

1. capture screenshot images from the archive,
2. preprocess images for contrast and text clarity,
3. run Tesseract to recover text,
4. compare OCR output to the original screenshot,
5. mark uncertain passages for human verification,
6. record recurring problems in a log.

## Example Tesseract command

```bash
tesseract input.png stdout --psm 6
```

## Why manual verification is still necessary

The archive contains screenshots with reduction, cropping, and visual artifacts that cause frequent problems in OCR output. Common issues include:

- misread words such as “Meberships” instead of “Memberships”,
- line breaks inserted into titles,
- weak capitalization in headings,
- truncation of date or contact details,
- confusion between service names and event titles.

## Recovery sample

The sample text files in the repository show the difference between raw OCR output and a verified version. This distinction matters because it demonstrates how automated extraction can produce useful drafts without replacing thorough human review.

- Raw OCR sample: [../../data/archive/recovered_text/sample-home-ocr.txt](../../data/archive/recovered_text/sample-home-ocr.txt)
- Verified sample: [../../data/archive/recovered_text/sample-home-verified.txt](../../data/archive/recovered_text/sample-home-verified.txt)
- Error log: [../../data/ocr_error_log.csv](../../data/ocr_error_log.csv)

## Recommended standard

For a future rebuild, only pages with a high-confidence OCR result should be treated as production-ready without manual review. Any page containing contact details, dates, donation content, or staff information should receive a human check before being published.
